Novo (NYSE:NVO) has faced significant challenges over the past couple of years. The company's shares have dropped by more than 60% as a result. However, the drugmaker is looking for ways to recover. Management set several goals for 2030 that could enable Novo to improve its financial results. Let's look into whether Novo can achieve these goals and deliver competitive returns over the next few years.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Novo's master plan

Novo's recent challenges stem from the fact that it generates most of its money from its GLP-1 products, including Wegovy, Ozempic, and Rybelsus. However, it has lost market share in this area to Eli Lilly (NYSE:LLY).

Novo wants to make up ground in this market while also diversifying its lineup and pipeline over the next few years. By 2030, Novo aims to have more than five products generating several billion dollars in annual sales each. All three GLP-1 products mentioned above fit that description, at least as of last year, but they will likely encounter significant competition over the medium term.

Novo will have to launch at least several brand-new products to reach its goal, and some of its candidates look promising. For instance, the company is awaiting approval for CagriSema. This drug mimics the action of the GLP-1 and amylin hormones and beat Wegovy in a head-to-head Phase 3 study in obesity.

CagriSema looks promising, as do several other products Novo is working on. The company's zenagamtide, a next-gen diabetes and obesity product, is being tested in Phase 3 clinical trials after posting outstanding early-stage results.

Both CagriSema and zenagamtide appear to have blockbuster potential, and several other candidates should enter late-stage studies over the next few years. So, this goal is achievable for Novo. There are others.

The company will also seek to have at least five Phase 3 diabetes and obesity programs in its pipeline by 2030, as well as at least five Phase 3 programs in other therapeutic areas. But what will Novo's financial performance through 2030 look like? The company aims to grow its revenue at an annual rate comparable to that of its industry peers.

Top-line growth in the high-single-digit or low-double-digit percentages is typically considered good for pharmaceutical giants. Another exciting goal Novo is looking to achieve by 2030 is to expand its capacity to serve 10 times as many obese patients with oral GLP-1 products and reach more than 60 million patients in total. For context, the company reached over 45.6 million patients last year.

Extending the 4.5% rise it enjoyed from the close of trading on Tuesday through the end of yesterday's trading session, Howmet Aerospace (NYSE:HWM) stock is climbing higher after the company announced third-quarter 2026 financial results that exceeded expectations. And with the aerospace parts manufacturer providing an auspicious outlook for the last quarter of 2026, investors have found even more reason to bid the stock higher.

As of 3:14 p.m. ET, Howmet shares are up 4.7%.

Image source: Getty Images.

Raising 2026 guidance has a funny way of making investors sit up and take notice

Growing revenue 29% year over year, Howmet reported sales of $2.7 billion -- better than the $2.58 billion that analysts had anticipated. Similarly, the company reported adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $1.46, surpassing the consensus among analysts that it would report $1.37.

Besides the income statement, investors found cause for celebration in the company's cash flow statement. In Q3 2026, Howmet generated free cash flow of $562 million, a 32.9% of that which it reported during the same period last year.

Updating its 2026 outlook, management now projects revenue of $10.29 billion to $10.31 billion, up from its previous projection of about $10.05 billion. Plus, Howmet expects to generate stronger free cash flow in 2026 than initially thought: $1.95 billion to $2.05 billion, compared with the previous guidance of approximately $1.9 billion.

Howmet's core business centers on manufacturing engine components, fastening systems, and airframe structural components for aerospace, defense, and gas turbine applications.

Is now the time to take flight with Howmet stock?

While Howmet stock trades at 42.1 times trailing earnings, it's hard to say that shares are inexpensive, but this industrial stock commands a higher valuation considering the company's consistently strong performance. With Howmet shares down 28.2% over the past three months, investors may want to load up before they start to soar.

title: Why Fortinet Stock Plunged More Than 20% Today
detail:
Why Fortinet Stock Plunged More Than 20% Today
Neha Chamaria, The Motley Fool
Thu, October 29, 2026 at 4:09 PM EDT 3 min read
FTNT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Fortinet (NASDAQ:FTNT) just raised its full-year forecast for the third time this year. The cybersecurity stock still tanked, plummeting 22% as of 2:30 p.m. ET Thursday to its lowest level in nearly five months.

Fortinet makes money in two ways. It sells physical and virtual network security products, notably its FortiGate firewalls, and then charges recurring fees for services and subscriptions to keep those firewalls secure.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

It's a classic razor-and-blade model, where the company sells products at lower margins to get its gear onto customers' networks. Then it makes most of its profit on the subscriptions that follow.

Management now expects more revenue this year than it did three months ago. So why is the stock falling?

Image source: Getty Images.

Fortinet's Q3: the numbers you must know

The razors are in high demand. Product revenue jumped 37% year over year in the third quarter, as customers moved to higher-performing models at higher prices, and total revenue climbed 20%. Price hikes helped.

Billings rose 29% to $2.3 billion, reflecting strong future revenue potential.

The blades are the problem, or so the market thinks. Services made up over 65% of Fortinet's revenue and an even higher percentage of gross profits last year. That service revenue grew just 13% in Q3. Management also trimmed its full-year service revenue forecast. The cut was tiny, under 1% at the midpoint, but it was a cut nonetheless.

If you look at sequential growth, overall business cooled off. In Q2, revenue grew 26%, product revenue 52%, and billings 33%.

That leaves investors with an uncomfortable question: Are Fortinet's high-flying days over?

What this means for Fortinet stock

Fortinet shares had climbed 120% this year before earnings stalled the rally. Any sign of a cooling off was bound to hit the stock price.

Investors, perhaps, interpret the service guidance cut as a sign that enterprise spending, or customers moving onto Fortinet's platform, could slow next year. The fear rippled across the industry and pulled other cybersecurity stocks down as well.

Fortinet isn't the kind of company to write off based on one quarter. Management expects billings to grow about 28% this year and revenue about 20%. It also lifted its full-year earnings forecast and boosted its buyback program by $1.2 billion.

Alex Carchidi, The Motley Fool

The privacy coin Zcash (CRYPTO: ZEC) has a pretty good shot at making big gains in 2027, and it might even make some of its investors rich in the process.

It's largely because AI is turning the issue of crypto security into a nightmare that the coin has already experienced and subsequently awoken from. And even after having that nightmare and seeing its price crash this summer (more on that in a moment), it's up by 276% over the last 12 months.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

I predict that next year will see this coin continue to grow rapidly, making many of its holders much wealthier in the process. The argument for Zcash being priced much higher in 2027 starts with a story about a bug that bit its holders quite hard.

Image source: Getty Images.
Zcash's team fixed a severe counterfeiting bug in five days

One big crypto story of 2026 is that advanced AI models have been finding code flaws (and often exploiting them to steal money) faster than developer teams can patch them.

Zcash faced this fulminating cybersecurity crisis well ahead of its peers. On May 29, a security researcher used Anthropic's Opus 4.8 model to find a problem in Orchard, which at the time was Zcash's main shielded (encrypted) pool. That issue could have allowed attackers to mint an unlimited amount of counterfeit Zcash, and because that counterfeiting would have occurred within the private pool where the network hides the amounts and identities of transactors, it would have been undetectable.

Zcash's developers shipped a fix on June 1, and there's no evidence that the exploit was ever used. Nonetheless, Zcash's price fell more than 50% overnight once the solved problem was disclosed.

Its developers then launched Ironwood, a formally verified privacy pool that lets anyone audit ZEC's supply, on July 28. The entire saga lasted just 60 days.

Since then, Zcash's network has been hardened even further, while other blockchains have seen their ecosystems wither in the face of increasingly sophisticated, AI-equipped attackers stealing funds. In other words, even with the benefit of seeing competitors get hit hard and Zcash rapidly bolstering its own security using AI tools, most other developer teams in the space are still not fully reacting to the risks posed by AI.

That makes Zcash's team look a lot better by comparison, and it means investors can have at least a little confidence that future threats will be dealt with proactively rather than reactively.
